title: A quick prime test meets 561
hook: 561 = 3 × 11 × 17 is not prime. How often does Fermat's quick test notice?

knows: fast powers mod n by repeated squaring (squaring-shortcut)
two numbers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is 1
doesNotKnow: that a composite number can pass Fermat's primality test for every coprime base
that a stronger test, checking square roots of 1, catches it

misconception: If a^(n-1) leaves remainder 1 for a coprime base, then n is prime (or at worst the test fails for only a few bases).
objective: The learner can explain that 561 = 3 x 11 x 17 passes Fermat's test for all 320 coprime bases (a Carmichael number), and that the stronger Miller-Rabin test catches it because the squaring chain for base 2 (263, 166, 67, 1) contains 67, a square root of 1 other than 1 and 560, which cannot happen modulo a prime.

claims.text: For a prime n, a^(n-1) mod n = 1 for every base a coprime to n.
claims.source: Fermat's little theorem; CLRS 4e ch. 31 (Theorem 31.31 in 3rd ed. numbering). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node check (fc21b/flt.mjs): a^(p-1) mod p = 1 for every a in 1..p-1 for all primes p < 2000, 0 failures; the theorem itself is Fermat's little theorem (standard proof via a, 2a, ..., (p-1)a permuting the residues). CLRS theorem number from memory, not opened; the sentence does not rest on it.

claims.text: 561 = 3 x 11 x 17, and all 320 bases coprime to 561 give a^560 mod 561 = 1.
claims.source: Demo.tsx COPRIME / FERMAT_ONES computed in the lesson; builder re-ran it with BigInt in a separate node script (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs), 2026-10-14: 320 coprime bases, 320 give 1. phi(561) = 2 x 10 x 16 = 320. Matches brief cs.algorithms #69. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own BigInt node check (fc21b/fermat.mjs): 3*11*17 = 561; 320 bases in 1..560 coprime to 561; all 320 give a^560 mod 561 = 1. Matches Demo COPRIME / FERMAT_ONES.

claims.text: 561 is a Carmichael number, and the smallest one: Fermat's test cannot tell it from a prime.
claims.source: Carmichael (1910), 'Note on a new number theory function', Bull. AMS 16; OEIS A002997 (first term 561). Builder checked in node that no composite below 561 passes for every coprime base (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own brute force (fc21b/fermat.mjs): no composite n in 4..560 has a^(n-1) = 1 mod n for every coprime a; 561 does, so it is the smallest Carmichael number. Carmichael 1910 and OEIS A002997 not opened (oeis.org blocked by proxy); the sentence is verified by the computation, not the citation.

claims.text: The stronger test writes 560 = 35 x 2^4, starts at a^35 and squares 4 times. For the stage's bases the chains are 2: 263, 166, 67, 1, 1; 5: 23, 529, 463, 67, 1; 7: 241, 298, 166, 67, 1; 10: 439, 298, 166, 67, 1; 13: 208, 67, 1, 1, 1. In each, 67 squared leaves 1.
claims.source: Demo.tsx chain(); builder re-ran it in node (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs): base 2 gives [263, 166, 67, 1, 1]; 67^2 = 4489 = 8 x 561 + 1. Miller-Rabin as in CLRS 4e ch. 31 (WITNESS). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node check: 560 = 35 x 2^4; chain for base 2 = 263, 166, 67, 1, 1; 67^2 = 4489 = 8 x 561 + 1. Demo chain() gives the same; the reveal prints the chain up to the first 1 (263, 166, 67, 1), consistent. | REWORDED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): The reveal now quotes the chain of the base the learner last ran (cut after the stray root), not base 2. Builder's node run of chain() for 2, 5, 7, 10, 13 gives the five chains above. Unverified. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own BigInt check (fc24/fer.mjs): 560 = 35 × 2^4; chains 2: 263,166,67,1,1; 5: 23,529,463,67,1; 7: 241,298,166,67,1; 10: 439,298,166,67,1; 13: 208,67,1,1,1; 67^2 mod 561 = 1. Every stage base has a witness (67), so the reveal always prints the chain cut after the 1 and '67 squared leaves 1' for whichever base strongFor holds (no Reset clears it).

claims.text: Modulo a prime, only 1 and n - 1 square to 1, so a different square root of 1 proves the number composite.
claims.source: x^2 = 1 mod p means p divides (x - 1)(x + 1), so p divides one factor: x = 1 or x = p - 1. CLRS 4e ch. 31 (Corollary 31.35 in 3rd ed. numbering). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Re-derived: x^2 = 1 mod p means p | (x-1)(x+1), so x = 1 or p-1. Own node check: no nontrivial square root of 1 modulo any prime < 2000. CLRS corollary number from memory, not opened; not relied on.

claims.text: The stage offers bases 2, 5, 7, 10 and 13; each gives a^560 mod 561 = 1, and the stronger test catches 561 with each of them.
claims.source: Chosen bases (disclosed per pattern disclose-chosen-seeds): picked as small coprime bases that are not strong liars. Chains from node: 5: 23, 529, 463, 67, 1; 7: 241, 298, 166, 67, 1; 10: 439, 298, 166, 67, 1; 13: 208, 67, 1, 1, 1 (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Own node chains: 5: 23,529,463,67,1; 7: 241,298,166,67,1; 10: 439,298,166,67,1; 13: 208,67,1,1,1. Each has a value other than 1 or 560 squaring to 1 (witness), and each gives a^560 = 1 (Fermat). Matches Demo BASES and witnessAt().

claims.text: A few bases still slip past the stronger test (10 of the 320 here, about 3%), so several random bases make a miss on 561 very unlikely.
claims.source: 9 strong liars among bases 2..560 coprime to 561 (50, 101, 103, 256, 305, 458, 460, 511, 560; base 1 excluded), Demo.tsx LIARS and builder's node script. Bound: at most 1/4 of bases are strong liars for any odd composite n > 9 (Rabin 1980, J. Number Theory 12; Monier 1980); CLRS 4e ch. 31 proves a 1/2 bound. Each extra independent random base multiplies the error chance by at most 1/4. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): DISPUTED. Own node check: counting all 320 coprime bases, 10 are strong liars: 1, 50, 101, 103, 256, 305, 458, 460, 511, 560. Demo LIARS excludes base 1 (9) but divides by all 320, so '9 of the 320' is wrong. Fix (builder): either '10 of the 320' or '9 of the 319 bases from 2 to 560' (change LIARS or the denominator in the reveal). The quarter bound (Rabin 1980; Monier 1980) cited from memory, papers not opened; 10/320 is well under 1/4 here. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, W-192): Was '9 of the 320'. LIARS in Demo.tsx now counts all 320 coprime bases, base 1 included (base 1: a^35 = 1), giving 10: 1, 50, 101, 103, 256, 305, 458, 460, 511, 560; reveal reads '10 of 320'. Needs an independent check. · Fact-check pass 23 2026-10-14: Number fixed: own BigInt check gives 10 strong liars among the 320 coprime bases (1, 50, 101, 103, 256, 305, 458, 460, 511, 560), matching LIARS. DISPUTED on 'never more than a quarter': counted the lesson's way (of the coprime bases), n = 9 has 2 strong liars (1, 8) of 6 = 1/3; the Rabin-Monier bound is phi(n)/4 for odd composite n > 9 (own scan of odd composites below 4,000: max 1/4 apart from n = 9). The papers were not opened. Fix (builder): 'never more than a quarter for odd numbers above 9', or 'never more than a quarter of the bases from 1 to n - 1' (n = 9: 2 of 8). | REWORDED v3 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): Disputed in pass 23 on 'never more than a quarter' (n = 9). The general bound rests on Rabin and Monier, which nobody could open, so it is dropped. What remains is 561-only: LIARS = 10 of 320 (pass 23 own BigInt count), 10/320 = 3.1%, shown as Math.round = 3%. If k bases are drawn at random from the coprime ones, the chance all are liars is (10/320)^k (derivation, independent draws with replacement). Unverified. | FC pass 24 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Own BigInt count: 320 coprime bases, 10 strong liars (1, 50, 101, 103, 256, 305, 458, 460, 511, 560) = LIARS; 10/320 = 3.1%, Math.round -> 3%. 'Several random bases make a miss very unlikely' rests on the 561-only derivation (independent draws: (10/320)^k, e.g. 1e-3 for 2 bases, 3e-8 for 5); the dropped Rabin-Monier bound is no longer relied on.

recall.question: A number n gives a^(n-1) mod n = 1 for every base you try. What can you conclude?
options: It may still be composite; a stronger test is needed
recall.why: Carmichael numbers such as 561 pass Fermat's test for every coprime base. The Miller-Rabin test also looks for square roots of 1 other than 1 and n - 1, which only composites have.
